events.title: Release of the first System of National Accounts (SNA 1953)
events.description: The first official version of the System of National Accounts was published, using Gross National Product (GNP) as the headline indicator.
events.supporting_text: The first two official versions of the System of National Accounts (1953 and 1968) used the indicator Gross National Product (GNP).

significance.justification: Shows the early accounting framework using GNP, indicating that national‑account metrics can evolve.
significance.supporting_text: The first two official versions of the System of National Accounts (1953 and 1968) used the indicator Gross National Product (GNP).

events.title: Release of the second System of National Accounts (SNA 1968)
events.description: The second official version of the System of National Accounts was published, continuing to use Gross National Product (GNP) as the headline indicator.
events.supporting_text: The first two official versions of the System of National Accounts (1953 and 1968) used the indicator Gross National Product (GNP).

significance.justification: Reinforces that the SNA framework is mutable and can adopt different headline indicators.
significance.supporting_text: The first two official versions of the System of National Accounts (1953 and 1968) used the indicator Gross National Product (GNP).

events.title: Adoption of GDP as the headline indicator in the System of National Accounts (SNA 1993)
events.description: In the 1993 edition of the System of National Accounts, Gross Domestic Product (GDP) replaced GNP as the primary headline indicator.
events.supporting_text: Later on, in the SNA 1993, GDP was adopted and GNP was sidelined.

significance.justification: Marks the institutional shift that entrenched GDP as the dominant economic metric.
significance.supporting_text: Later on, in the SNA 1993, GDP was adopted and GNP was sidelined.

events.title: Quarterly lock‑up procedure for BEA GDP reporting
events.description: A recurring, quarterly lock‑up process in which Bureau of Economic Analysis statisticians work in a secure room to compile and approve the United States GDP report before it is released to the public.
events.supporting_text: a group of civil servants go into the "lock-up" procedure in a secure room at 4600 Silver Hill Road, Maryland, USA... This procedure is followed every quarter.

significance.justification: The highly restrictive, opaque process sustains GDP dominance and limits transparency needed for metric reform.
significance.supporting_text: They are not allowed to leave... All computers have been disabled for outside communication... The report includes a key indicator called Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

events.title: First edition of the System of National Accounts (SNA) released
events.description: The inaugural edition of the international handbook System of National Accounts (SNA) was published, led only by the United Nations with a small number of active countries and experts.
events.supporting_text: The SNA has only been revised four times in the last seventy years (1953, 1968, 1993, 2008)... For the first two editions of the SNA the number of active countries/experts was small and was led only by the UN.

significance.justification: Shows the early, limited governance of the SNA, highlighting the baseline infrastructure that underpins GDP‑centric measurement.
significance.supporting_text: For the first two editions of the SNA the number of active countries/experts was small and was led only by the UN.

events.title: Second edition of the System of National Accounts (SNA) released
events.description: The second edition of the System of National Accounts (SNA) was published, still under the leadership of the United Nations with limited participation from member states.
events.supporting_text: The SNA has only been revised four times in the last seventy years (1953, 1968, 1993, 2008)... For the first two editions of the SNA the number of active countries/experts was small and was led only by the UN.

significance.justification: Reinforces the early, narrowly‑participated SNA framework that continues to shape GDP measurement.
significance.supporting_text: For the first two editions of the SNA the number of active countries/experts was small and was led only by the UN.

events.title: Third edition of the System of National Accounts (SNA) released
events.description: The third revision of the System of National Accounts (SNA) was issued, marking a later update to the international methodology for measuring economic activity.
events.supporting_text: The SNA has only been revised four times in the last seventy years (1953, 1968, 1993, 2008).

significance.justification: Illustrates the slow, incremental evolution of the SNA, maintaining the status‑quo of GDP‑based accounting.
significance.supporting_text: The SNA has only been revised four times in the last seventy years (1953, 1968, 1993, 2008).

events.title: Fourth edition (2008 update) of the System of National Accounts (SNA) released
events.description: The most recent revision of the System of National Accounts (SNA) was completed in 2008, involving participation from all countries and international institutes, and updating the 722‑page manual on recording economic transactions and resources.
events.supporting_text: The System of National Accounts (SNA), which was last updated in 2008... In the last revision, the SNA 2008, all countries and all the international institutes were involved.

significance.justification: Marks a broader, more inclusive revision that could enable future shifts away from GDP‑centric metrics.
significance.supporting_text: In the last revision, the SNA 2008, all countries and all the international institutes were involved.

events.title: Simon Kuznets' 1934 statement on the limits of GDP as a welfare measure
events.description: Simon Kuznets, a pioneer of national accounting, publicly noted that national income (GDP) does not reliably indicate a nation's welfare, highlighting early recognition of GDP's limitations for measuring societal success.
events.supporting_text: Simon Kuznets, one of the pioneers of national accounting, famously wrote in 1934 that "the welfare of a nation ... can scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income".

significance.justification: Kuznets’ quote directly critiques the prevailing use of GDP as a proxy for welfare.
significance.supporting_text: “the welfare of a nation ... can scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income” (1934).

events.title: Ascendance of GDP as a national income metric
events.description: GDP began to be used as an innovative economic indicator in the 1930s, rapidly increasing its market share and reaching a peak in the innovation curve, illustrating the classic Schumpeterian stages of early adoption, take‑off, saturation and decline.
events.supporting_text: The blue line shows the ascendance of GDP, which started in the 1930s and has since made a spectacular move up this innovation curve.

significance.justification: Shows how GDP has become the dominant metric, a condition that sustains current economic focus away from nature.
significance.supporting_text: The blue line shows the ascendance of GDP, which started in the 1930s and has since made a spectacular move up this innovation curve.

events.title: Development of Beyond‑GDP initiatives
events.description: Initiatives that seek to move economic decision‑making beyond GDP have been active for several decades, currently situated on the upward portion of the innovation cycle but still far from their peak.
events.supporting_text: Beyond‑GDP initiatives have existed for several decades and are definitely on the upward curve of the innovation cycle.

significance.justification: Indicates an emerging alternative metric that could shift the system toward harmony with nature.
significance.supporting_text: Beyond‑GDP initiatives have existed for several decades and are definitely on the upward curve of the innovation cycle.

events.title: Adoption of the System of National Accounts (SNA)
events.description: The System of National Accounts was adopted in 1953, providing a standardized set of concepts and rules for measuring national economies and leading to rapid harmonisation of national income accounting worldwide.
events.supporting_text: The SNA has, since 1953, prescribed what concepts to use when measuring the economy. ... After the adoption and implementation of the SNA, worldwide national income accounting was harmonised rapidly.

significance.justification: Standardising accounting opened space for new macro‑economic metrics beyond GDP.
significance.supporting_text: After the adoption and implementation of the SNA, worldwide national income accounting was harmonised rapidly.

events.title: 2008 Financial Crisis
events.description: A global financial crisis that triggered widespread mistrust among citizens toward economic models, policies, and data advocated by economists.
events.supporting_text: Similarly, in the wake of the 2008 crisis citizens' mistrust in the models, policies and data advocated by economists started to grow again.

significance.justification: The crisis triggered growing public mistrust in economists and their models.
significance.supporting_text: in the wake of the 2008 crisis citizens’ mistrust in the models, policies and data advocated by economists started to grow again.

events.title: Development of the System of National Accounts (SNA) common language
events.description: The creation and diffusion of a shared macro‑economic language (the SNA) that enabled greater institutionalisation of economic thought and the formation of a global macroeconomic community.
events.supporting_text: The development of a common language was crucial in the increased institutionalisation of economic thought and for creating a macroeconomic community.

significance.justification: The common language enabled a macroeconomic community and institutionalised economic thought.
significance.supporting_text: The development of a common language was crucial in the increased institutionalisation of economic thought and for creating a macroeconomic community.

events.title: Ongoing criticism of GDP as an economic indicator
events.description: A continuous process of criticism of GDP's adequacy that has been present since the 1930s, raised by economists and non‑economists who argue that GDP does not measure well‑being, inequality, sustainability or environmental impacts.
events.supporting_text: Since national income started in the 1930s, there has been criticism from economists and non‑economists.

significance.justification: The text foregrounds persistent scholarly and professional critique of GDP, revealing the current dominance of a flawed metric.

events.title: Publication of the Brundtland Report (Our Common Future)
events.description: Seminal publication that introduced and institutionalised the term “sustainable development”, defining it as development that meets present needs without compromising future generations.
events.supporting_text: This is the underlying philosophy of the Brundtland Report which was the seminal publication that led to the institutionalisation of the term sustainable development as "development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs".

significance.justification: The report introduced and institutionalised the concept of sustainable development, opening a pathway for systemic change.
significance.supporting_text: The underlying philosophy of the Brundtland Report which was the seminal publication that led to the institutionalisation of the term sustainable development

events.title: Adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
events.description: All United Nations member states formally adopted a list of 169 targets (the SDGs), providing a worldwide, politically‑backed framework that could be leveraged by the Beyond‑GDP community. In 2015 the Sustainable Development Goals were introduced, defining 17 goals and 169 targets for sustainable development, representing a worldwide agreement.

events.title: Long‑term process to develop and implement the System of Global and National Accounts (SGNA) as a replacement for GDP
events.description: A multi‑year effort described in the book to design, pilot, and institutionalise a new accounting framework (the SGNA) that will replace GDP by the target year 2030. The process includes drafting the architecture, defining sub‑accounts, creating quality indicators, and planning implementation and institutionalisation.

significance.supporting_text: Part II ... this is a long‑term process that will only be fully completed by 2030.

events.title: Publication of "The Income of Nations" by Studenski
events.description: Studenski’s 1958 book provides a near‑encyclopaedic overview of national income accounting from 1665‑1958, marking a key scholarly output on the history of GDP.
events.supporting_text: The first, covering the years 1900 to 1958, is derived from The Income of Nations by Studenski (1958), which provides a nearly encyclopaedic overview of national income accounting for the period 1665-1958.

events.title: United Nations begins collection of national accounts data
events.description: The UN started systematically gathering national accounts statistics from member states, initiating a global data‑collection effort that expanded the availability of GDP‑related information.

events.title: Passage of U.S. Congressional Resolution 220 requesting national income statistics
events.description: On 8 June 1932, Representative Robert La Follette Jr. secured a majority vote for Resolution 220, which formally requested the Department of Commerce to compile national income statistics for the period 1922‑1932.
events.supporting_text: It took until 8 June 1932 before La Follette could get a majority to vote for resolution 220 which requested national income statistics for the period 1992-1932.

significance.justification: The resolution mandated government‑led statistical work, enabling systematic national‑income measurement.
significance.supporting_text: it took until 8 June 1932 before La Follette could get a majority to vote for resolution 220 which requested national income statistics.

events.title: Publication of Simon Kuznets’ report to the U.S. Congress
events.description: Kuznets delivered a landmark report on national income estimates to Congress on 4 January 1934, providing the first comprehensive macro‑economic data requested during the Great Depression.
events.supporting_text: A case in point is one of the landmark publications in the history of national accounting: a report by Simon Kuznets on 4 January 1934.

significance.justification: The widely read report raised public awareness of macro‑economic indicators.
significance.supporting_text: The report was definitively noticed by the press and the public. It sold 4,500 copies at $0.20 a copy.

events.title: Bretton Woods Conference
events.description: The 1944 Bretton Woods meeting established a new international monetary system, replacing the gold standard with dollar‑pegged currencies and creating the IMF and World Bank.
events.supporting_text: The international economic order changed significantly at the Bretton Woods meeting in 1944, ushering in a new economic era with the gold standard being replaced by a system in which currencies were pegged to the US dollar.

significance.justification: The conference reshaped the global economic order, creating institutions that could alter how growth is measured and pursued.
significance.supporting_text: The international economic order changed significantly at the Bretton Woods meeting in 1944, ushering in a new economic era...

events.title: Founding of the Organisation for European Economic Co‑operation (OEEC)
events.description: The OEEC was established in 1948 to coordinate the distribution of Marshall Aid and to foster economic recovery in post‑war Europe.
events.supporting_text: Initially called the Organisation for European Economic Co‑operation (OEEC), it was founded in 1948 and played an important role in the post‑war economic recovery of Europe.

significance.justification: OEEC coordinated post‑war economic recovery and data collection across Europe.
significance.supporting_text: Initially called the Organisation for European Economic Co‑operation (OEEC), it was founded in 1948 and played an important role in the post‑war economic recovery of Europe.

events.title: Establishment of the United Nations
events.description: The United Nations replaced the League of Nations in 1945, becoming the primary global intergovernmental organization for peace, security, and international cooperation.
events.supporting_text: The ineffective League of Nations was replaced by the United Nations in 1945.

significance.justification: Replacing the League of Nations created a new platform for global coordination, including statistical cooperation.
significance.supporting_text: the ineffective League of Nations was replaced by the United Nations in 1945.

events.supporting_text: In 1949, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) was agreed.

significance.supporting_text: In 1949, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) was agreed.

events.title: Founding of the European Economic Community

significance.supporting_text: The European Economic Community, a forerunner of the European Community, was founded in 1957.

events.description: The United States’ Marshall Plan (1948‑1952) provided large‑scale financial assistance to rebuild European economies, spurring the production of regular national accounts for aid allocation.

events.title: OECD pledges 50 % GDP increase for member countries by 1970
events.description: In 1961 the OECD set an international growth target, committing its members to raise aggregate GDP by 50 % by the year 1970.
events.supporting_text: In 1961, this target setting was elevated to an international goal: the OECD pledged a 50 per cent increase in GDP of OECD countries by 1970.

significance.justification: The pledge cemented GDP growth as a central policy target, shaping public and political discourse.

events.title: Van Lennep’s 1970 statement on recession risk
events.description: OECD Secretary‑General Van Lennep publicly asserted that major recessions were no longer inevitable, emphasizing the role of policy miscalculation.
events.supporting_text: In 1970, Van Lennep, the Secretary‑General of the OECD, reported that "A major recession would no longer be a deus ex machina, but could only result from miscalculation or a deliberate act of government".

significance.justification: The statement framed recessions as preventable, reinforcing the primacy of growth‑oriented policy.
significance.supporting_text: In 1970, Van Lennep, the Secretary‑General of the OECD, reported that “A major recession would no longer be a deus ex machina, but could only result from miscalculation or a deliberate act of government”.

events.title: Presidential address to the American Economic Association by Robert Lucas
events.description: Robert Lucas, Nobel Prize winner and founder of the new classical school, delivered his presidential address to the American Economic Association, stating that macroeconomics had solved the problem of depression prevention.
events.supporting_text: Robert Lucas, Nobel Prize winner and founder of the new classical school, said during his presidential address to the American Economic Association in 2003: "My thesis in this lecture is that macroeconomics in this original sense has succeeded: Its central problem of depression prevention has been solved, for all practical purposes, and has in fact been solved for many decades."

significance.justification: Lucas’s address declares macroeconomics solved depression, reinforcing the prevailing focus on growth and GDP.

concepts.name: System of National Accounts (SNA)
concepts.definition: An international handbook that provides methodological guidelines for recording economic transactions and resources of a society; it defines how GDP and related aggregates are calculated.
key_proponents: All member states of the European Union
concepts.supporting_text: These are recorded in an international handbook called the System of National Accounts (SNA), which was last updated in 2008. It is a 722‑page manual on how to record the economic transactions and resources of a society.
supporting_texts: These are recorded in an international handbook called the System of National Accounts (SNA), which was last updated in 2008. It is a 722‑page manual on how to record the economic transactions and resources of a society.

"In this book, the term GDP is used to refer to the headline indicator of the national accounts... The first two official versions of the System of National Accounts (1953 and 1968) used the indicator Gross National Product (GNP). Later on, in the SNA 1993, GDP was adopted... The SNA includes other macroeconomic aggregates such as Gross National Income (GNI)."

The System of National Accounts is the foundation upon which modern empirical macroeconomics is built. The SNA has, since 1953, prescribed what concepts to use when measuring the economy. After the adoption and implementation of the SNA, worldwide national income accounting was harmonised rapidly. ... it can be seen as a "language" because it contains the definitions of macroeconomic terms (dictionary) and also their relationships (grammar).

The SNA provides a common language which (macro)economists all over the world speak. Whether the native language of a macroeconomist is Swahili, Urdu or Portuguese, they can "speak" to their fellow (macro)economists using their SNA language. In fact, many of the terms have gradually percolated into society and media. Consumption, investment, productivity and capital are just a few terms which have society-wide use.
The SNA itself phrases this as follows: "Per capita volumes of major aggregates are often used as a measure of the relative standard of living in countries..."
It should not be implemented in rich developed countries first and then slowly permeate towards developing countries, as was the case for the SNA.
Macroeconomic statistics started to harmonise into the System of National Accounts, with the first edition being published in 1953 (more on the SNA later in this chapter).

In 1953, Stone was the principal author of the first ever UN handbook, which is considered the first "official" SNA. This document provided a global harmonised system of national accounts... The SNA is thus the formalisation of the "language of macroeconomics".
Thirdly, macroeconomists have agreed on a formal macroeconomic language: the System of National Accounts. The language has proven to be versatile and has survived shifts in macroeconomic theory.

significance.justification: SNA is the statistical framework that institutionalises GDP measurement.
significance.supporting_text: "structured around a science (macroeconomics), a statistical framework (SNA) and a key indicator (GDP)."

significance.supporting_text: The social indicator movement ... aimed to overcome the dominance of economic indicators. The main result was a major boost in the measurement of subjective well‑being.

concepts.name: Easterlin paradox
concepts.definition: The observed empirical finding that higher income levels do not necessarily translate into higher levels of happiness or subjective well‑being.
concepts.supporting_text: The importance of subjective well‑being measures was further bolstered by the academic discussion about the Easterlin paradox in the early 1970s.

significance.justification: Shows that higher income does not automatically increase happiness, questioning GDP as a welfare metric.
significance.supporting_text: The importance of subjective well‑being measures was further bolstered by the academic discussion about the Easterlin paradox in the early 1970s.

concepts.name: Beyond‑GDP initiatives
concepts.definition: Collective efforts and alternative measurement systems that aim to assess societal progress and wellbeing beyond the traditional Gross Domestic Product metric.
concepts.supporting_text: The next couple of sections will provide a more detailed overview of the various Beyond‑GDP initiatives.

significance.justification: Collectively represent a systemic shift away from GDP‑centric accounting.
significance.supporting_text: Typology of Beyond GDP Methodologies

concepts.name: Social indicators movement
concepts.definition: A historical movement in the early 1970s that promoted the development and use of social measures, such as subjective well‑being surveys, to complement economic statistics.
concepts.supporting_text: SWB survey life evaluations got a boost from the "social indicators movement" in the early 1970s.

significance.justification: Highlights earlier attempts that fell short of establishing a full alternative framework.
significance.supporting_text: the “social indicators movement” in the early 1970s.

concepts.name: U‑index
concepts.definition: A metric that records the percentage of time an individual spends on unpleasant activities, quantifying wellbeing by measuring the proportion of negative experiences.
concepts.supporting_text: Kahneman and Krueger (2006) suggest that any episode can be quantified as positive or negative. Based on this, they propose the "U-index", which records the percentage of time spent on unpleasant activities.

significance.justification: Introduces a quantifiable indicator of unpleasant time, expanding the toolkit for well‑being measurement.
significance.supporting_text: Based on this, they propose the “U-index”, which records the percentage of time spent on unpleasant activities.

concepts.name: Eudaimonia (well‑being dimension)
concepts.definition: A deeper psychological dimension of wellbeing that refers to motivations such as competence, engagement, meaning, optimism, positive relationships, resilience, self‑esteem, emotional stability and vitality.
concepts.supporting_text: The third SWB approach, Eudaimonia, refers to deeper psychological motivations such as Competence, Engagement, Meaning, Optimism, Positive relationships, Resilience, Self‑esteem, Emotional stability and Vitality.

significance.justification: Adds deeper psychological dimensions to well‑being, broadening the scope of alternative metrics.
significance.supporting_text: The third SWB approach, Eudaimonia, refers to deeper psychological motivations such as Competence, Engagement, Meaning...

concepts.name: Measure of Economic Welfare (MEW)
concepts.definition: The first prominent green‑accounting aggregate, created in 1972, that adds the value of leisure time and home production to a macro‑economic aggregate and subtracts monetary estimates of environmental damage to provide a better estimate of economic welfare.
concepts.supporting_text: That was the year the Measure of Economic Welfare was created by Yale economists Nordhaus and Tobin. This was the first prominent example of a "green accounting" aggregate.

significance.justification: Introduces a new aggregate that adjusts GDP to better reflect welfare, showing a pathway to systemic metric change.
significance.supporting_text: This was the first prominent example of a “green accounting” aggregate… The idea is that the aggregate index provides a better estimate of economic welfare.

concepts.name: Index for Sustainable Economic Welfare (ISEW)
concepts.definition: A green‑accounting indicator inspired by the MEW, proposed in 1989, that adjusts traditional economic aggregates for environmental and social factors to estimate sustainable economic welfare.
concepts.supporting_text: The MEW methodology inspired the Index for Sustainable Economic Welfare (ISEW), which was proposed in 1989 by Daly and Cobb.

significance.justification: Shows the evolution of green accounting concepts beyond MEW toward more comprehensive welfare measures.
significance.supporting_text: The MEW methodology inspired the Index for Sustainable Economic Welfare (ISEW), which was proposed in 1989 by Daly and Cobb.

concepts.name: genuine savings indicator
concepts.definition: A capital‑approach metric, suggested in 1993, that records the net additions to the various stocks of capital (produced, financial, human, natural, social), treating investments in education as increases in human capital and depletion of natural resources as reductions in capital stock.
concepts.supporting_text: Based on this capital theory, the genuine savings indicator was suggested in 1993. This indicator shows the additions to the various stocks of capital. For example, an investment in education is recorded as an increase in human capital while depletion of natural resources is a reduction in a capital stock.

significance.justification: Quantifies changes in capital stocks, linking economic activity to natural and human capital preservation.
significance.supporting_text: Based on this capital theory, the genuine savings indicator was suggested in 1993. This indicator shows the additions to the various stocks of capital.

concepts.name: Wealth accounting
concepts.definition: A conceptual approach that treats sustainability as the summation of monetised capital stocks; it gained prominence in the 1990s and is popular at the World Bank.
key_proponents: Working Group for Statistics on Sustainable Development (WGSSD)
concepts.supporting_text: The group built on the idea of wealth accounting, which had gained prominence in the 1990s and is also popular at the World Bank.
supporting_texts: The group built on the idea of wealth accounting, which had gained prominence in the 1990s and is also popular at the World Bank.
One can also measure the total value of each stock, which is known as wealth accounting.

significance.justification: Serves as a conceptual foundation for the WGSSD and later reports.
significance.supporting_text: The group built on the idea of wealth accounting, which had gained prominence in the 1990s.

concepts.name: adjusted net savings
concepts.definition: A World Bank‑published indicator that adjusts traditional net savings for investments in human capital, depletion of natural resources, and other environmental factors, reflecting a more comprehensive view of wealth creation.
concepts.supporting_text: This variety of green accounting is influential because the World Bank has adopted this approach and publishes "adjusted net savings" and "total (or comprehensive) wealth" indicators.

significance.justification: Published by the World Bank, institutionalising a green‑accounting metric for global use.
significance.supporting_text: The World Bank has adopted this approach and publishes “adjusted net savings” … indicators.

concepts.name: total (or comprehensive) wealth
concepts.definition: A World Bank indicator that aggregates the value of all forms of capital—produced, financial, human, natural, and social—into a single measure of a nation's comprehensive wealth.
concepts.supporting_text: This variety of green accounting is influential because the World Bank has adopted this approach and publishes "adjusted net savings" and "total (or comprehensive) wealth" indicators.

significance.justification: World Bank publication spreads a comprehensive wealth measure, supporting systemic adoption.
significance.supporting_text: The World Bank has adopted this approach and publishes … “total (or comprehensive) wealth” indicators.

concepts.name: Inclusive Wealth Index (IWI)
concepts.definition: An index that aggregates the value of produced, human, natural, and social capital to assess a country's inclusive wealth and sustainability over time.
concepts.supporting_text: The United Nations University, under the leadership of Partha Dasgupta, proposed the Inclusive Wealth Index (IWI).

significance.justification: Introduces an integrated wealth metric that captures natural, human, and produced capital.
significance.supporting_text: The United Nations University, under the leadership of Partha Dasgupta, proposed the Inclusive Wealth Index (IWI).

concepts.name: sustainable development (conceptual equivalent)
concepts.definition: A conceptual framing that equates the maintenance of a non‑declining stock of capital (including natural capital) with the broader notion of sustainable development.
concepts.supporting_text: This is sometimes seen by economists as the conceptual equivalent of the term "sustainable development".

significance.justification: Highlights how the capital approach is framed within the prevailing discourse of sustainable development.
significance.supporting_text: This is sometimes seen by economists as the conceptual equivalent of the term “sustainable development”.

concepts.name: capital approach (green accounting)
concepts.definition: A methodological approach that starts from the premise that society possesses various assets—produced, financial, human, natural, and social capital—and assesses welfare by ensuring these capital stocks are maintained or enhanced over time.
concepts.supporting_text: This method starts from the premise that society has certain assets (produced, financial, human, natural and social capital).

significance.justification: Introduces a distinct methodological strand that treats assets as capital, expanding green‑accounting theory.
significance.supporting_text: A third variety of green accounts emerged … based on a different economic method, the capital approach.

concepts.name: Carbon footprint
concepts.definition: An indicator derived from the ecological footprint that quantifies the amount of land (or forest) required to absorb the carbon dioxide emissions generated by fossil‑fuel use.
concepts.supporting_text: It has also led to the development of other related indicators, such as the carbon footprint, water footprint and material footprint.

significance.justification: Adds a climate‑dimension to the ecological footprint framework.
significance.supporting_text: It has also led to the development of other related indicators, such as the carbon footprint

concepts.name: Water footprint
concepts.definition: A related indicator that translates water consumption into the amount of water‑related bioproductive area needed to sustain that use.
concepts.supporting_text: It has also led to the development of other related indicators, such as the carbon footprint, water footprint and material footprint.

significance.justification: Extends the footprint approach to water use, highlighting resource interdependencies.
significance.supporting_text: water footprint

concepts.name: Material footprint
concepts.definition: A related indicator that expresses the total material extraction required to satisfy a country’s consumption, expressed as an area of productive land.
concepts.supporting_text: It has also led to the development of other related indicators, such as the carbon footprint, water footprint and material footprint.

significance.justification: Broadens the accounting to material extraction and use.
significance.supporting_text: material footprint

concepts.name: Biocapacity
concepts.definition: The total biologically productive area available within a region or the world, used as a reference against which the ecological footprint is compared.
concepts.supporting_text: Communicatively, the ecological footprint works very well because it can be contrasted to the biologically productive area available within a region or the world (biocapacity).

significance.justification: Provides the ecological ceiling against which footprints are compared.
significance.supporting_text: contrasted to the biologically productive area available within a region or the world (biocapacity)

concepts.name: Life Situation Index (LSI)
concepts.definition: An early composite index produced in the 1970s that aggregates multiple sub‑components to provide a single measure of societal well‑being, though it is not based on a conceptual framework.
concepts.supporting_text: For example, in the early 1970s the Life Situation Index (LSI) was produced in the Netherlands.

significance.justification: Early composite indicator that attempted to capture wellbeing beyond income.
significance.supporting_text: Life Situation Index (LSI)

concepts.name: Capability approach
concepts.definition: A philosophical framework that argues welfare should be measured not only by achieved functionings but also by the capabilities people have to lead the lives they value.
concepts.supporting_text: It is loosely based on Sen's capability approach. This framework argues that welfare should not only be measured according to realisations of people's lives (functionings) but also the potential people have to live the life that they want (capabilities).

significance.justification: It offers a theoretical foundation that can shift welfare measurement from purely economic to multidimensional wellbeing.
significance.supporting_text: The capability approach… critiques welfare economics… argues that welfare should be measured by functionings and capabilities.

concepts.name: Gross National Happiness
concepts.definition: A Beyond‑GDP initiative that measures multiple dimensions of wellbeing through a population survey; it was initiated by the King of Bhutan in the early 1970s.
concepts.supporting_text: One of the earliest and most cited Beyond‑GDP initiatives is the programme on Gross National Happiness which was initiated by the King of Bhutan in the early 1970s.

significance.justification: Early, high‑profile alternative to GDP that inspired later beyond‑GDP initiatives.
significance.supporting_text: One of the earliest and most cited Beyond‑GDP initiatives is the programme on Gross National Happiness which was initiated by the King of Bhutan in the early 1970s.

concepts.name: Millennium Development Goals (MDGs)
concepts.definition: A set of development targets that ran from 2000 to 2015 and were replaced by the Sustainable Development Goals.
concepts.supporting_text: At that conference, it was decided that the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs), which ran from 2000 to 2015, would be replaced by the SDGs.

significance.justification: Identifies the prior global framework that was later superseded by the SDGs.
significance.supporting_text: At that conference, it was decided that the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs), which ran from 2000 to 2015, would be replaced by the SDGs.

concepts.name: Better Life Index (BLI)
concepts.definition: An OECD‑launched indicator set that can be aggregated into a single index; it starts with equal weights for each indicator but allows users to customise weights via a web‑based application.
key_proponents: Organisation for Economic Co‑operation and Development (OECD)
concepts.supporting_text: An influential indicator set is the Better Life Index (BLI), which was launched by the OECD at its fiftieth anniversary.

significance.justification: Allows users to set their own weights, encouraging participatory measurement.
significance.supporting_text: An influential indicator set is the Better Life Index (BLI), which was launched by the OECD at its fiftieth anniversary.

concepts.name: Conceptual Indicator Sets (Type 4)
concepts.definition: Indicator sets built on explicit conceptual frameworks rather than purely stakeholder‑driven processes; early adopters include Switzerland, Norway, New Zealand, the Netherlands and Belgium.
concepts.supporting_text: In the mid‑2000s a couple of countries started to create indicator sets based on conceptual frameworks: Switzerland, Norway and New Zealand. Later the Netherlands and Belgium also introduced Type 4 indicator sets.

significance.justification: Limited adoption but noted as influential for harmonisation efforts.
significance.supporting_text: Although the number of countries which have adopted these indicator sets is limited, Type 4 has been influential in the various harmonisation efforts.

concepts.name: System of Environmental and Economic Accounting (SEEA)
concepts.definition: A modular accounting framework that produces both physical and monetary environmental indicators, originally developed as a “satellite” account for the environment and now regarded as a statistical standard on an equal footing with the System of National Accounts (SNA).
concepts.supporting_text: The final Beyond‑GDP initiative that will be discussed in this chapter is the SEEA. This is a successful initiative which is hard to classify because it is an accounting framework that produces both Type 1 and Type 4 indicators… The SEEA 2012 – Central Framework was adopted by the Statistical Commission of the United Nations… The SEEA has the same standing as the SNA since they are both "statistical standards"… The European Commission made it legally binding for all European countries to produce six of the SEEA accounts.

significance.justification: Recognised as a statistical standard, giving it legitimacy.
significance.supporting_text: The SEEA has the same standing as the SNA since they are both “statistical standards”.

concepts.name: eco‑domestic product (EDP)
concepts.definition: A green accounting indicator obtained by subtracting environmental costs from Net Domestic Product.
concepts.supporting_text: The SEEA 1993 includes a green accounting indicator called the eco‑domestic product (EDP) which is obtained by subtracting environmental costs from the Net Domestic Product.

significance.justification: Provides a concrete alternative to GDP that accounts for environmental costs.
significance.supporting_text: The SEEA 1993 includes a green accounting indicator called the eco‑domestic product (EDP) which is obtained by subtracting environmental costs from the Net Domestic Product.

concepts.name: physical accounts
concepts.definition: Components of the SEEA that record the flows and stocks of an economy in mass and energy units, including resource use and emissions by industry.
concepts.supporting_text: The largest part of the SEEA handbook deals with the physical accounts which record the flows and stocks of an economy. This includes physical flows in terms of mass and energy units as well as resource use or emissions by industry.

significance.justification: Physical accounts provide the data needed to understand and manage resource flows, enabling systemic shifts toward environmental limits.
significance.supporting_text: The largest part of the SEEA handbook deals with the physical accounts which record the flows and stocks of an economy.

concepts.name: depletion‑adjusted net value added
concepts.definition: A green accounting aggregate proposed by the SEEA that deducts consumption of fixed capital and depletion from gross value added.
concepts.supporting_text: The SEEA also proposed green accounting aggregates called "depletion‑adjusted net value added" … which are obtained by deducting consumption of fixed capital and depletion from gross value added.

significance.justification: Introduces a new aggregate that internalises resource depletion, opening a pathway to change accounting practice.
significance.supporting_text: The SEEA also proposed green accounting aggregates called “depletion‑adjusted net value added”...

concepts.name: depletion‑adjusted net domestic product
concepts.definition: A green accounting aggregate proposed by the SEEA that deducts consumption of fixed capital and depletion from GDP.
concepts.supporting_text: The SEEA also proposed green accounting aggregates called … "depletion adjusted net domestic product", which are obtained by deducting consumption of fixed capital and depletion from gross value added and GDP.

significance.justification: Provides an adjusted GDP metric that can shift economic evaluation toward sustainability.
significance.supporting_text: … “depletion adjusted net domestic product”, which are obtained by deducting consumption of fixed capital and depletion...

concepts.name: environmental macroeconomics
concepts.definition: A community and emerging field that seeks to manage the economy within environmental limits, using a common language such as the SEEA framework.
concepts.supporting_text: The goal of this community is to manage the economy within environmental limits… The SEEA is in a good position to become the "common language" for environmental macroeconomics.

significance.justification: Positions the SEEA as a common language for a discipline aimed at managing economies within environmental limits.
significance.supporting_text: The SEEA is in a good position to become the “common language” for environmental macroeconomics.

concepts.name: satellite account
concepts.definition: A methodological approach that treats environmental accounts as a separate, supplementary set of accounts linked to the core System of National Accounts rather than integrating them directly into the core framework.
concepts.supporting_text: It was decided that rather than put environmental aspects and social issues into the "core" SNA framework, it was better to allow for a "satellite" account for the environment.

significance.justification: Shows the compromise of keeping environmental data peripheral to the core SNA, limiting integration.
significance.supporting_text: it was decided ... better to allow for a “satellite” account for the environment.

concepts.name: macroeconomic community
concepts.definition: The established economic community centred on GDP, described as more powerful than the well‑being and sustainability community.
concepts.supporting_text: the macroeconomic community is more powerful than the well‑being and sustainability community.

significance.justification: Identified as a powerful, dominant bloc that overshadows alternative efforts.
significance.supporting_text: The macroeconomic community is more powerful than the well‑being and sustainability community.

concepts.name: System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting (SEEA)
concepts.definition: An accounting framework that provides a clear goal, structure and common language for integrating environmental and economic information; highlighted as the most successful example in the Beyond‑GDP scene.
concepts.supporting_text: The SEEA is probably the most successful example in the Beyond‑GDP scene. It has a clear goal, structure and common language (SEEA), and the harmonisation process took less than twenty years.

significance.justification: Serves as a structured, standardized accounting system that can replace GDP‑centric metrics.
significance.supporting_text: The SEEA is probably the most successful example in the Beyond‑GDP scene.

concepts.name: Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) process
concepts.definition: An international, goal‑oriented process that has demonstrated the ability of global institutes to foster agreement on sustainability and wellbeing metrics.
concepts.supporting_text: The SDG process also proved that international institutes can be very effective in fostering a global agreement.

significance.justification: Demonstrates how international institutions can mobilise agreement around alternative goals.
significance.supporting_text: The SDG process also proved that international institutes can be very effective in fostering a global agreement.

concepts.name: Motivational Interviewing (MI)
concepts.definition: A therapeutic approach that engages addicts in a positive discussion of their goals, motives and futures; proposed by Costanza et al. as a model for addressing society’s ‘addiction’ to GDP.
concepts.supporting_text: For example, Motivational Interviewing (MI) is based on engaging addicts in a positive discussion of their goals, motives and futures. Costanza and colleagues explore what the MI therapy might look like if applied to society's addiction to GDP.

significance.justification: Suggested as a novel therapeutic approach to change societal attachment to GDP.
significance.supporting_text: Costanza and colleagues explore what the MI therapy might look like if applied to society’s addiction to GDP.

concepts.name: addiction to GDP
concepts.definition: A metaphorical framing that likens society’s focus on economic growth to a real addiction, suggesting that the same methods used to treat addicts could be applied at the societal level.
concepts.supporting_text: Costanza et al. (2017) liken society's focus on economic growth to a real addiction.

significance.justification: Frames GDP dominance as a pathological condition that needs to be addressed.
significance.supporting_text: Costanza et al. (2017) liken society’s focus on economic growth to a real addiction.
